newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia eyes reforms to boost foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia eyes reforms to boost foreign investment.

text.p: Mongolia will soon pass a package of economic reforms to improve the climate for foreign investment in the remote north Asian nation, Minister of Finance Tsagaan said.
The Great Hural, or parliament, would pass a series of measures by the middle of next year aimed at removing obstacles to attracting overseas capital, he told Reuters in a recent interview.
"A lot of changes will be elaborated in the tax laws, foreign investment laws, mining laws and other relevant laws," Tsagaan said.
"Conditions (for investment) will be more favourable, more transparent, more efficient and less bureaucratic," he added.
High taxes and customs duties, an anaemic banking system and a cumbersome bureaucracy are some of the problems facing investors in Mongolia.

Many foreign investors attending an economic roundtable in Ulan Bator also complained to Tsagaan of legal confusion in many areas such as investment protection, property development and property rights.
"There are a lot of unclear issues," one Western investor told Reuters after the seminar. "Foreign investors do not really know what they are getting into."
The government would work to implement the changes before the start of an international oil, gas and mining investment seminar planned for June of next year, Tsagaan said.
"Investors will see a change towards a positive direction."
Foreign investment in Mongolia totalled $123 million by the end of October, official figures show.
Most companies in Mongolia are subject to a 40 percent income tax although investors in some sectors, such as mining, can enjoy tax holidays of several years.
An import duty of 26.5 percent is levied on all imports, including equipment.
Interest rates for the rare credits granted to Mongolia's private sector fluctuate between six and 10 percent a month.
Foreign companies are not allowed to buy land but may lease it for up to 60 years with a right to extend beyond that. Leases are not transferable.

But many investors said they were confident the new reformist government that swept into power in June with a dramatic victory over the former Communist Party was ready to forge ahead with the badly needed changes.
"The prime minister is a man of action, he will move quickly," another foreign businessman said.
